chapters.title: Chapter 4: Kelly Sizing in Indian F&O and Multi-Asset Portfolios

lessons.title: Case Study: Covariance-Adjusted Kelly for a Five-Stock Portfolio

children.text: Lesson 4.3's closed-form formula worked because it only had to handle two assets. A five-stock portfolio needs the general version, f* = Σ⁻¹μ, computed in code from a real covariance matrix. This case study builds that matrix carefully, computes f* for all five positions at once, and sizes the resulting portfolio.

Five illustrative Nifty 50 large-caps across different sectors: HDFC Bank, Infosys, Reliance Industries, Hindustan Unilever and Maruti Suzuki. Every expected return, volatility and correlation figure below is an illustrative planning assumption, not a verified historical statistic or forecast.
Building a Covariance Matrix That Is Actually Valid

Picking five pairwise correlations by hand risks building a matrix that is not mathematically valid: a covariance matrix has to be positive semi-definite, and an arbitrary set of correlations can easily fail that test. A one-factor model sidesteps this entirely. Assume each stock's return is driven partly by the market and partly by its own idiosyncratic movement:

body.caption: M is the market return, ε_i is idiosyncratic noise, and D is a diagonal matrix of each stock's idiosyncratic variance

children.text: This construction guarantees a valid covariance matrix by design, and it matches how correlation actually arises between large-caps in practice: they share exposure to the same market, plus their own sector- and company-specific noise. Assume Nifty's own volatility is 15%.

body.caption: Building Σ from the factor model, then computing f*
body.code:
import numpy as np

tickers = ["HDFC Bank", "Infosys", "Reliance", "HUL", "Maruti"]
beta    = np.array([1.1, 0.8, 1.0, 0.5, 1.2])
sigma   = np.array([0.22, 0.24, 0.25, 0.18, 0.26])
mu      = np.array([0.09, 0.07, 0.08, 0.05, 0.10])
sigma_m = 0.15

idio_var = sigma**2 - (beta * sigma_m)**2      # each stock's idiosyncratic variance
D = np.diag(idio_var)
Sigma = sigma_m**2 * np.outer(beta, beta) + D    # guaranteed valid covariance matrix

f_star = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) @ mu
standalone_k = mu / sigma**2

for t, f, k in zip(tickers, f_star, standalone_k):
    print(f"{t:12s}  portfolio f* = {f*100:5.1f}%   standalone k = {k*100:5.1f}%")

body.caption: Portfolio-adjusted f* vs standalone Kelly, from the code above

body.title: Verify one standalone figure
body.prompt: Using k = μ/σ², what is Reliance Industries' standalone Kelly fraction with μ = 8% and σ = 25%?
body.explanation: k = 0.08 ÷ 0.25² = 0.08 ÷ 0.0625 = 1.28, or 128%. This is the fraction the formula would suggest if Reliance were the only position held; the table shows the portfolio-adjusted figure drops to 39.4% once its correlation with the other four positions is accounted for.

body.text: Summing the standalone column gives 737.7% of capital. Summing the portfolio-adjusted column gives 305.4%, a reduction of well over half. All five stocks share real exposure to the same market factor, so a large part of each one's standalone edge is redundant with the others. The covariance-adjusted formula finds and removes that redundancy; naive summation cannot.

body.title: Why the portfolio sum is so much smaller
body.question: The portfolio-adjusted sum (305.4%) is far below the naive sum of standalone fractions (737.7%). What best explains this gap?
options: The five stocks have negative expected returns
All five stocks share substantial exposure to the same underlying market factor, making their standalone edges partly redundant with each other
The covariance matrix used in the calculation is mathematically invalid
Position sizing formulas always shrink dramatically once more than two assets are involved
body.explanation: Every stock in this portfolio has meaningful beta to Nifty, so a large share of the risk in each one is the same shared market risk, not five independent sources of risk. Σ⁻¹μ correctly identifies and removes this overlap. This is specific to how correlated these particular five stocks are, not a universal shrinkage rule for any five-asset portfolio.

children.text: Apply quarter-Kelly to the portfolio-adjusted fractions, and convert to rupee targets for a ₹25,00,000 account.

body.text: This totals ₹19,09,000, about 76% of the account, deployed across five names rather than concentrated in one. Lesson 3.2's table showed quarter-Kelly for a single diversified Nifty position at a similar total figure, 78.13%, but that put the entire amount behind one exposure. Here, a shock specific to any single company, an earnings miss, a regulatory action, a product recall, only threatens its own slice of the ₹19,09,000, not the whole amount. Matching the total percentage deployed is not the same as matching the actual concentration risk being taken.

points: For more than two assets, f* = Σ⁻¹μ is computed in code from an explicit covariance matrix, not worked out by hand.
A one-factor model (r_i = β_i M + ε_i) is a reliable way to build a covariance matrix that is guaranteed mathematically valid, rather than picking correlations arbitrarily.
Summing standalone Kelly fractions overstated this portfolio's true optimal leverage by more than double, because all five stocks share substantial market-factor exposure.

Portfolio-level sizing does not just reduce total leverage; it also spreads concentration risk across multiple sources of edge rather than one, even when the total percentage of capital deployed looks similar to a single-position example.
This closes Chapter 4's progression: single defined-risk options in 4.1, single leveraged futures in 4.2, two correlated assets in 4.3, and a full multi-asset portfolio here.
